analysis.one_liner: Lets generic drug makers sue brand manufacturers that refuse to sell them samples needed to develop cheaper copies.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan bill, with 25 cosponsors split almost evenly between the parties, sat in two House committees for 20 months and died without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Before a company can sell a cheaper generic version of a drug, it must test its copy against the original. Some brand-name manufacturers refuse to sell samples of their drugs to generic developers, which delays cheaper competition for years. This bill would let generic developers go to court and force a sale on market terms, with fines and attorney fees if the brand company stalled without a legitimate reason. It also gives regulators clearer power to let generic makers use their own patient-safety procedures instead of being forced into slow negotiations with the brand company over shared safety programs.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and taxpayers who end up paying brand-name prices for years when generic competition is delayed; generic drug developers, who get a faster way to obtain samples and win attorney fees when a brand company stalls.

how_it_helps.text: Generic and biosimilar developers could sue a brand manufacturer that refuses to sell sufficient quantities of its drug on commercially reasonable, market-based terms, and a court could order the sale without delay.

If a brand company delayed without a legitimate business justification, the court could award the generic developer attorney fees and a penalty of up to the revenue the brand earned on the drug during the delay period.

The bill would let the Health and Human Services Secretary approve a generic maker's own safety protections for drugs with restricted-distribution programs, ending bad-faith negotiations over shared safety systems that the bill says are used to delay generic approval.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, which would lose the ability to stretch out monopoly-priced sales by withholding samples, and would face court orders, fees, and penalties when they do.

drawbacks.text: Brand manufacturers and the FDA have argued that some drugs are restricted for safety reasons, and distributing them outside the shared safety program could pose risks to patients; the bill responds by requiring the Secretary to authorize sample access and comparable safety protections, but opponents see litigation and safety friction as the price.
The bill creates a new stream of lawsuits with mandatory attorney fees, which some argue could be used to pressure manufacturers even in close cases.
The remedy only helps where sample refusal is the bottleneck; it does nothing about the many other ways brand companies delay generic entry, so its benefit is real but narrow.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a specific, documented obstacle to generic competition: FDA's own drug center director testified that some manufacturers use safety-program and distribution restrictions as reasons not to sell samples, and the FTC chair raised the same concern. The cost is added litigation and some safety-process complexity, largely managed by the Secretary-authorization and liability-limit provisions. On balance, the gains — faster cheaper generics for patients and taxpayers — outweigh the costs, though the fix covers only one of several tactics used to delay generics.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Judiciary committees the day it was introduced, sent to the Health Subcommittee, and neither committee ever acted on it before Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 27, 2017 by Rep. Tom Marino with Rep. David Cicilline as co-introducer.
It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the House Judiciary Committee, and on April 28, 2017 sent to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action through the end of the 115th Congress on January 3, 2019.
It gathered 25 cosponsors, 13 Democrats and 12 Republicans.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers, which kept the ability to slow generic competitors by refusing to sell samples — with patients and taxpayers continuing to pay brand prices in the meantime.

for.name: Rep. Tom Marino
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to let generic developers sue brand manufacturers that withhold samples.

for.name: Rep. David Cicilline
for.what_they_did: Joined Rep. Marino in introducing the bill.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the complete action history shows no further action after the subcommittee referral.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and never acted on it.

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA)
against.what_they_did: Opposed the CREATES Act, arguing existing antitrust law was sufficient and that the bill's sample-access mandate created safety and litigation problems.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start: a Republican sponsor introduced it with a Democratic co-introducer, and its 25 cosponsors split 13 Democrats and 12 Republicans.

industries.note: The bill ends their ability to delay generic competition by refusing to sell samples or by dragging out negotiations over shared safety programs, and exposes them to court orders, attorney fees, and penalties up to the revenue earned during the delay. Brand monopoly pricing on those drugs would erode faster.
They gain a tailored civil action to obtain test samples on market terms and a clearer regulatory path to use their own safety procedures, letting them bring lower-cost copies to market sooner.

industries.industry: Health insurers and government health programs
industries.note: Faster generic entry lowers drug prices, which the bill's findings say saves patients and taxpayers billions of dollars each year; insurers, Medicare, and Medicaid pay less.
